name: Agreement with the Yuma (Quechan), December 4, 1893, ratified August 15, 1894
nations: Quechan (Kwatsáan) Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation
promises: Upon the conditions expressed, the Yuma Indians relinquished their reservation established by executive order of January 9, 1884 (28 Stat. 332-333).

The Supreme Court describes the agreement as one that could be read to condition the cession of a 25,000-acre tract of boundary lands on the United States building an irrigation canal within three years, allotting irrigated land to individual Indians, selling certain lands to pay for the canal, and opening certain lands (Arizona v. California, 2000).

breaches.what: Interior Solicitor Leo Krulitz concluded that the 1893 Agreement made a conditional cession of the disputed lands, that the United States had not met the conditions, and that title is held by the United States in trust for the Quechan. The Secretary of the Interior adopted that opinion by Secretarial Order, except for lands acquired under Acts of Congress or conveyed to third parties, reversing the Department's 1936 Margold and 1977 Austin opinions that the cession was unconditional. The Supreme Court calls the order an admission that the agreement had been ineffective to transfer title.

breaches.what: The Quechan claim in Docket 320, which had alleged the agreement was obtained by fraud and coercion and that the United States failed to perform it, was settled by a consent judgment of $15 million, stated not to be an admission by either party.

landTaken: The Supreme Court describes a 25,000-acre tract of boundary lands as the disputed part of the cession (530 U.S. 392).
compensation: The 1983 settlement of Docket 320 paid the tribe $15 million for the claims in that docket (530 U.S. 392).
today: In Arizona v. California (2000) the Supreme Court held that neither its 1963 decision nor the 1983 consent judgment barred the Quechan and the United States from claiming water rights for the disputed boundary lands, and recorded that both continue to recognize the tribe's entitlement to those lands.

openQuestions: The Krulitz opinion and the 1978 Secretarial Order were not opened directly; they are cited as the Supreme Court sets them out.
The 1978 order excepted lands the United States had acquired by Act of Congress or conveyed to third parties; how much of the 25,000 acres it returned in fact was not found.

The Quechan Tribe's website (quechantribe.com/about-us) gives no account of the 1893 agreement; the nation voice is missing. Press accounts (Yuma Sun) describe the signing as fraudulent; not cited here.
Docket 319 (aboriginal lands) is a separate claim, recorded on cession-1884-01-09-yuma.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): breach wording checked against Arizona v. California, 530 U.S. 392, 404-405 (2000). The Krulitz opinion is dated January 2, 1979 (86 I.D. 3) but the Court says it was issued in 1978 and adopted by the Secretarial Order of December 20, 1978; 'reversing the 1936 Margold opinion' widened to Margold and the 1977 Austin opinion, which had reaffirmed it; the order's exception for lands acquired by Congress or conveyed to third parties added; the Court's own word 'admission' added. Plain no longer says 'about 25,000 acres still belong' to the tribe, since the order excepted some parcels. The 1983 consent judgment stays litigation.

plain.promised: In 1893 the Quechan gave up their 1884 reservation in return for irrigated allotments, a canal within three years and other conditions.
plain.happened: In 1978 the Interior Department concluded the conditions were never met and that the boundary land, apart from some parcels already conveyed or acquired by Congress, is still held in trust for the Quechan. The tribe's claim was settled in 1983.
plain.today: The tribe received $15 million in 1983. In 2000 the Supreme Court let it seek water rights for the boundary lands.
